A head and shoulders profile portrait of one of the most important and well-known early twentieth century Luo leaders, Chief Ogada of Kisumu clan, seated on a European chair against the backdrop of the administrative building in Kisumu. His hide body covering is elaborately decorated with small beads. Ogada gave Hobley a detailed description of his personal ornaments as seen in this photograph, including stone neck beads (tik ng’ut), bead and metal earrings (ngaga) and armlets (minyonge). His cleanly shaved head is strange since chiefs covered their heads with head gear as a sign of authority. [Gilbert Oteyo 21/04/2005 &  CM 24/04/2007]

A group of Luo warriors at Karungu in South Nyanza in full warrior dress with long spears and shields, as well as large headdresses of colobus monkey tail hair and ostrich plumes, posed in a rocky landscape. The adornment and the shields are typical of the late nineteenth and early twentieth century period for the Luo. [Gilbert Oteyo 06/05/05 & CM 27/04/2007]

These are Luo women going fishing with fishing basket traps (osech kiteng'a - osera means 'woven fishing trap' and kiteng’a is the fishing method of covering the fish in the water with this trap, with its pointed end upwards). Kiteng'a was always a fishing method for women only. The traps are made of those ropes seen being made in 1998.209.44.1 - .2 and they are usually carried on the head like this. These women are standing probably at the entrance of their homestead, which is apparently planted with some young banana trees. Their personal body adornments include wrist bracelets (minyonge), glass neck beads (tikng’ut) and glass waist beads (tik nungo). Three of the ladies wear skin or cloth aprons (olemo) on the front while the one to the extreme right wears a fibre tail (chieno) to her rear, suggesting that they are young married women. Unmarried ladies were traditionally not keen on kiteng’a fishing, which was done mostly by married women. [Gilbert Oteyo 06/05/05]

A group portrait of a seated woman surrounded by young women and younger girls, and described as belonging to Kisumu clan of the Luo, captured in a humorous moment in relaxed fashion despite the posed formality of the group. Their personal adornments are simple glass bead necklaces (tik ng’ut), front aprons (olemo), string waist belt and waist beads (tik nungo) and earrings (stadi). The shaven head hair styles are very youthful and would have been a fashion in the period for young women. [Gilbert Oteyo 06/05/05]

This group is a mixture of married Luo women, young girls and children, posed in a line standing and seated, at Karungu in south Nyanza. Here the use of  skin or fibre aprons (olemo), armlets (minyonge) and bead necklaces (tik ng’ut) is very evident, and in fact some girls and women have adopted a whole waist skin wrap. [Gilbert Oteyo 06/05/05 & CM 27/04/2007]

A portrait of a Luo man wearing bead ornaments around the neck and waist, an upper arm leather/hide bangle, metal leg rings and armlets (minyonge) and a skin apron both at the back and front. The man is sitting on a stool in front of a colonial administrative building, almost certainly at the newly established centre in Kisumu. The building is carefully constructed from local materials, including bundles of lake reeds surrounding the roof supports to form an open verandah, and stone work beneath.  [Gilbert Oteyo 24/04/2005 CM 24/04/2007]

This is a scene of bull fighting where mature bulls fight it out to determine who controls the heard, particularly the cows. The bull owner also takes the clan and village pride of having the powerful bull and musicians can sing praises of him. The herd is seen to the side. The location could be Nyanza, but not necessarily Luo country. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]
A portrait of a youth standing in the yard of a colonial station in mountainous country. The location is uncertain, but probably Kenya. [CM 23/04/2007]

A formal group photograph of Luo men in European clothing outside a large thatched building. Note also four different kinds of western hats (not helmets) worn by some of them.  Some are seated on a wooden bench outside the thatch house, which is only partially seen but seems to fit some of the colonial administrative bomas built for administration purposes in rural areas. It could be even a local African administrator’s home. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]
Looking down from a ridge across large boulders towards Lake Kanyaboli. [CM 13/03/2007]

A group portrait of a household head (identified as John) seated outside his house with an older son (identified as Absalom) and three smaller children all in European clothing. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]
A view of Uyoma village in Alego Location, with a number of homesteads (mier) visible in the open and shrubby landscape. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]
A view of Uyoma village in Alego Location, with a number of homesteads (mier) visible in the open and shrubby landscape. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

According to its original caption, this photograph was taken in connection with a ruined Luo stonewalled settlement of a type known as ohinga to archaeologists of the region, possibly at Kanyipir village. Such ruins are common in Luo country, particularly in South Nyanza District. Many of these settlements date to the nineteenth century and some may be contemporary with the earthwork settlements known as gunda bur, elsewhere photographed by Evans-Pritchard. The three men posing for the camera are unidentified, but they all appear to be in the employ of the colonial administration due to their clothing. The one on the left is wearing a chief's helmet (simba) and may be the man called Okoth identified in 1998.349.213. The man in the middle appears in 1998.349.215 while the other two appear in 1998.349.213. [Gilbert Oteyo & CM 11/04/2007]
A view of a bird in grass beside a path running up to a large colonial house. Evans-Pritchard had a keen and lifelong interest in birds. [CM 16/04/2007]
A man wearing a waist cloth walking towards the camera, with another wearing a colonial uniform standing to the left, location uncertain.  [CM 16/04/2007]

A portrait of a Luo girl, her arm holding the shoulder of a woman (out of frame) with a child below her elbow, at Gangu village. The village scene is typical with a homestead vegetation fence and banana plants in the background, while a sisal plant is at the bottom right corner. The woman on the left is mostly out of frame but one can see part of her bead necklace (tick ngut) probably of glass beads and a wrist ring (minyonge) on her left wrist. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]
A woman walking down a tree-lined road with a basket on her head. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

Man playing an eight-stringed musical instrument (nyatiti). He is wearing a feather headdress (kondo udo, ostrich feathers) stuck on a plaited mat hat and has a wrap of stringed metal jingles (gara) on his right leg. He has a metal toe ring (oduong’o) to hit the wooden harp bar for a particular musical sound to be made. On the finger is worn another metal ring (tere) which may be just a personal body ornament. He is seated in front of a grass thatch house with some banana plants and a thick homestead fence in the background. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

Women and children with baskets and pot on their heads (slightly out of focus). The meaning of the original record 'Kisio women' is obscure, and may be a variant of a village name in Luo country. The woman in the centre is wearing wrist rings (minyonge) on both wrists. These women and children are probably on their way to, or coming from a market. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

An upper body portrait of a man (identified as Ezekiel Onyango) wearing European shirt and jacket, a stick under his left arm. Onyango was a local colonial chief living in Kadimo village in Yimbo location at the time of Evans-Pritchard's visit.

Lake Kanyaboli is a well known lake in Luo land and is mainly in Alego Location, as well as Sakwa and Yimbo Locations. The lake is a swamp lake formed by water from the River Yala. This river starts in the Western Kenya highlands and runs through most of Siaya District of Nyanza Province before emptying into a swamp also called Yala Swamp. The water tends to seep through the swamp into this lake which does not therefore allow the River Yala to actually drain into Lake Victoria. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

Women dancing at a funeral ceremony called tero buru (driving death away). This is usually a ceremony after burial where people shout and curse death, rigorously running and dancing to drive away bad spirits from the home of a deceased person. Although women are dancing here and one would ordinarily say that this may be a woman’s funeral, in related images to this one a large number of cattle can seen being driven beyond the women by men with shields, and it would seem therefore that this is the tero buru of a respectable elder. The dancers are all women clad in headdresses and woven dancing tails (chieno) made of vegetable fibre. Their bodies are meticulously decorated with smears of soil or ochre of varying colours. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

Looking from the top of a ridge towards Kendu Bay, a small township in South Nyanza District. It is on the shore of Lake Victoria and had a small pier and a steamship service connecting it with Kisumu. The clear plain area and lake shore area of it is seen here with the lake water in the distance. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]
An upper body portrait of a young Luo man wearing a European shirt standing in front of a thatched house. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

A group of school children at a school in Mulaha Village, Ugenya Location, Siaya District. They are all in school uniform with the older children standing behind and the younger of junior classes sitting in front. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

This is a view of Luo open countryside with gentle hills and open valleys in Ugenya Location, Siaya District. fenced Luo homesteads as can be seen here are set on the gentle hill as the open valleys are farmed. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

A portrait of a Luo woman (possibly identified as Lenya) from Gangu village, wearing a beadwork headdress (ligisa). The ligisa headdress is open at the top, made of vegetable fibre and sticks, and decorated with glass beads (tigo). She is also smoking tobacco using a long stem (ondhuru) connected to a clay pipebowl (kwesi). Her forehead is also decorated with scarification spots (ngo’l) in horizontal parallel lines (see also 1998.349.113). Behind her is a plantation of a type of sorghum (bel) showing their grain heads and probably ready for harvesting. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

A view of Luo country from a hillside, with a man in the foreground leaning on a stick. He is standing next to a substantial stone boundary wall (ohinga) which can be seen curving away to the right. This may be Alego or Ugenya Location. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004 & CM 16/03/2007]

This is a view of a Luo settlement earthwork called gunda bur (gunda being a abandoned home, bur the bank and ditch). People lived within the earthwork where houses were built and cattle were tethered, protected by the bank and ring-ditch (created by the excavation of earth to build up the bank). These structures were built by the Luo at the beginning of the 1700s and some remained occupied until the late 1800s. In the original notes, this photo is described as the 'old bur Asembo' and I am inclined to think that this is one of the old settlement locations of the Asembo clan. Many of these spectacular earthworks still exist in Asembo location up to this present day. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004 & CM 16/03/2007]

Looking from the top of a ridge towards Kendu Bay, a small township in South Nyanza District. It is on the shore of Lake Victoria and had a small pier and a steamship service connecting it with Kisumu. The clear plain area and lake shore area of it is seen here with the lake water in the distance. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

Looking from the top of a ridge towards Kendu Bay, a small township in South Nyanza District. It is on the shore of Lake Victoria and had a small pier and a steamship service connecting it with Kisumu. The clear plain area and lake shore area of it is seen here with the lake water in the distance. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]
An upper body portrait of a man wearing a white shirt, identified as Sergeant Ezekiel. [CM 20/03/2007]

This is the landscape of the area around Kendu Bay in Karachuonyo Location, South Nyanza District. The terrain drops away from the hills above Kendu Bay into the open flat land towards the shore, with Lake Victoria seen in the far background. This is a densely settled area and Luo homesteads can be seen below, often spread out as groups of fenced homesteads with grass thatch huts, surrounded by thick euphorbia fences. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

This is the landscape of the area around Kendu Bay in Karachuonyo Location, South Nyanza District. The terrain drops away from the hills above Kendu Bay into the open flat land towards the shore, with Lake Victoria seen in the far background. This is a densely settled area and Luo homesteads can be seen below, often spread out as groups of fenced homesteads with grass thatch huts, surrounded by thick euphorbia fences. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

This is an earthwork of a typical Luo defended homestead enclosure dating to the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The dug ditch and bank structure is called bur in Luo, and an abandoned home is gunda, which gives the term gunda bur for this type of archaeological earthwork. People lived within the earthwork, where houses were built and cattle tethered, protected by both the earthwork and the surrounding ring ditch. In the original notes, this photo is described as the 'old bur Asembo' and I am inclined to think that this is one of the old earthwork settlements of the Asembo clan of the Luo. Many of these spectacular earthworks still exist in Asembo Location up to day. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004 & CM 23/03/2007]

A Luo warrior (or just a man going to a funeral) holding a spear and a hide shield. An animal hide/skin lap (pien) is hanging below the bottom of the shield. On his head is a Colobus monkey tail headdress (kondo bim). This attire is usually for warriors and those going to a funeral as they will perform the funeral ceremony tero buru there. Curious children are watching from behind. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

The schoolchildren of Mulaha School posed for a formal group photograph. Some of them are wearing the badge of the school on their uniform, a cross on a shield. It seems likely that they are posed formally like this due to the visit of Evans-Pritchard and his host Archdeacon Owen. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004 & CM 23/03/2007]

A portrait of a man seemingly identified as Mboya (or Mbuga) of Uhanya Village in Alego Location. On his head is the cowry shell hat ogut gagi which extends into a cowry shell necklace (tik gagi mar ngut) with glass beads (tigo). He has a finger ring which may be for tapping a smoking pipe (oduong’o) and quite a number of wrist rings (minyonge) on both wrists. His long pole (odunga) is of interest, and was often used when attending a funeral. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]
A car parked on a dirt road, packed with equipment. This is probably the car (registration number B 6895) used to transport Evans-Pritchard on his tour around Luo country in 1936. [CM 29/03/2007]

A typical Luo homestead (dala) with a thick euphorbia fence surrounding grass thatch huts, set on the upper slopes of the undulating Luo countryside. The rest of the village is seen spread over the landscape. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

This is an earthwork of a typical Luo defended homestead enclosure dating to the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The dug ditch and bank structure is called bur in Luo, and an abandoned home is gunda, which gives the term gunda bur for this type of archaeological earthwork. People lived within the earthwork, where houses were built and cattle tethered, protected by both the earthwork and the surrounding ring ditch. In the original notes, this photo is described as the 'old bur Asembo' and I am inclined to think that this is one of the old earthwork settlements of the Asembo clan of the Luo. Many of these spectacular earthworks still exist in Asembo Location up to day. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004 & CM 23/03/2007]

A school group in front of their classroom at Kagonya village school in Ugenya. The school building is a distinctive long rectangular grass thatch building divided into single rooms, possibly up to five classes. The children's shirts have a distinctive badge incorporating the letters 'SK' which may be a reference to the school name. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

A group of six  schoolchildren of Mulaha School posed for a photograph, one wearing the badge of the school on his uniform, a cross on a shield. It seems likely that they are posed like this due to the visit of Evans-Pritchard and his host Archdeacon Owen. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004 & CM 23/03/2007]

These men are building a Luo round house (ot). The construction starts with digging a round trench in which cut poles of different sizes are put and stabilized. Then the horizontal supports of usually young trees or split sisal are tied around them to hold them together as a wall (kor ot). Finally the last wall plate on which the roof (tado) will lie is done and woody vegetation placed in the wall vertically, which is what these men seem to be doing. The entire wall would then be plastered over with earth and cow dung both inside and outside. This plastering process is only done after the roof is put on, lest the rain spoil it. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004 & CM 03/04/2007]
An upper body portrait of a Luo man wearing a European shirt, with a pen clipped to it. [CM 03/04/2007]

This man is dressed in a long robe (kanzu or kandho) and wears a glass bead decorated hat (ogut tigo). This hat is only worn by men and not by women. Around his waist is a belt, probably of sisal fibre (okanda tworo), and he is holding his walking stick (luth) under his arm. On his feet he is wearing sandals made of animal hide or skin (wuoche pien). He is playing a wind instrument (oporo) which is made of animal horn at one end, and attached to a long hollow wood or bamboo pipe which he blows on the side. Such an instrument is usually played during funerals but also during other entertainment ceremonies. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]
This young man is identified as James and looks like a Luo who is really taking up a Western way of life. The compound behind him is also well planned and planted with trees. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]
A group portrait of three men from Kogelo Clan (Jokogelo) in Alego Location. Their names are not given but they look very Westernized from their clothing. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

An upper body portrait of a Luo man (identified as Absalom) wearing a European shirt, standing next to an open car door. Just visible standing to the left can be seen a young man, identified elsewhere as James. [CM 04/04/2007]
A group portrait of three Luo men wearing European clothing, identified from left as Absalom, Saul and Joshua.

This man is sitting on a wooden chair outside his grass thatch hut. He is clean shaved using an iron blade (nyamarich) except a small patch on top center of his head, He has an ostrich eggshell necklace (rek) and glass bead earrings of the type worn by men (ngaga). His clothing is simply of animal (cow?) skin (pien), which was a common Luo attire. Beyond him, looking back toward the camera is another man dressed in colonial service clothing. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]
An upper body portrait of a young Luo man in European dress, identified as James. [CM 04/04/2007]
An upper body portrait of a Luo boy standing in front of a thatched house, with the arm of another man just visible to the right of frame. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

This is a section of the Sondu River between Nyakach and Kabondo Locations in South Nyanza District. The Sondu River starts in the Nandi and Kipsigis highlands and flows down through the steep gorges of Nyakach and Kabondo Hills and into Lake Victoria in the southern part of Kavirondo (Winam) Gulf. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]
